clue.text: Smooth musician's 'Stranger on the Shore'? Certainly not

blocks.note: to sand wood is to smooth it
a piper is a musician who plays pipes

explanation.surface: A smooth player performing the clarinet hit 'Stranger on the Shore' — and someone scoffing at it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stranger on the Shore' is Acker Bilk's 1961 clarinet hit, which makes it look like a song title; read literally, the shore bird is anything but a stranger there.
explanation.definitionFit: A sandpiper is a wading bird that lives along beaches, so it is no stranger to the coast.

clue.text: River of soup – no hoax!

indicators.note: 'no' tells us the following word's letters are absent from the dish

blocks.note: consommé is a clear soup
a con is a trick or hoax

explanation.surface: A diner insisting the river-flavoured soup is genuinely made with river water.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking CON from the front of CONSOMME leaves SOMME.
explanation.definitionFit: The Somme is a river in northern France, famous for the First World War battle.

clue.text: Far from content, at loose end? Open out

indicators.note: 'out' suggests the letters are thrown out of their order and spread around anew

blocks.note: the letters of these words, taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone discontented and idle, being urged to open up and talk.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark breaks the fodder in the surface, but every letter of 'at loose end? Open' is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Being none too pleased is an understatement for being rather unhappy, the opposite of contented.

clue.text: Headgear with fashionable insert, reversed flap

indicators.note: the headgear is described as having something put inside it, so one piece sits within the other
'reversed' asks for the whole combination to be read from right to left

blocks.note: a cap is a hat
what's in is in fashion

explanation.surface: A hat with a trendy lining and a flap folded back the other way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flap' sits at the end looking like part of the hat, but it is the definition, in its sense of a fluster.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in a flap is to be in a state of agitation, so flap is a synonym for panic.

clue.text: See 2
One attending emergency (small house on Mull)

blocks.note: res is a short form of residence, a house
to mull something over is to ponder it

explanation.surface: Someone attending a crisis at a little cottage on the Scottish island of Mull.
explanation.walkthrough: Mull looks like the Hebridean island but is the verb 'think over'; 'small' signals a shortened word.
explanation.definitionFit: A responder, as in first responder, is a person such as a paramedic who answers an emergency call.

clue.text: See 26
Like K-9 in unstable orbit, circling round and around

indicators.note: something unstable will not stay fixed, so these letters fall into a new order
circling means going around, so the jumbled word wraps the next piece

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
O is round in shape
c. is the abbreviation of circa, around

explanation.surface: Doctor Who's dog K-9 spinning wildly in a wobbly orbit.
explanation.walkthrough: K-9 is the robot dog from Doctor Who. The rearranged ORBIT wraps O, then C, from circa, is added at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: K-9 is a mechanical dog, so being like it is being machine-like or robotic.

clue.text: Bound dictionary includes 'book with a gilt refinement'

indicators.note: a refinement reworks something into a better form, so these letters are reshaped
the dictionary includes the rest, so it is placed around it

blocks.note: the OED is the Oxford English Dictionary
B is the abbreviation for book
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A bound dictionary that boasts in its blurb of a gilded binding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound' looks like a description of the dictionary, but it is the definition; B plus rearranged A GILT sits inside OED.
explanation.definitionFit: To be bound to do something is to be obliged, or obligated, to do it.

clue.text: Distinction of contemporary artist with cash but no power

indicators.note: 'but no' says the money must go without one of its letters

blocks.note: Tracey Emin is a contemporary British artist
pence is cash, British coins
P is the symbol for power

explanation.surface: A wealthy but powerless modern artist's claim to distinction.
explanation.walkthrough: Tracey Emin is a famous British contemporary artist. P comes out of PENCE, leaving ENCE.
explanation.definitionFit: Eminence is prominence or high rank, a state of distinction.

clue.text: Delicate newspaper worker let off

indicators.note: 'off' as in gone off or awry, so the letters are out of order

blocks.note: a sub, or subeditor, checks copy at a newspaper
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A sensitive journalist being excused from duty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Let off' reads as a phrase meaning excused, but 'off' is working on 'let' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Subtle and delicate both describe something fine, faint or finely judged.

clue.text: With leaders of Commons and Lords involved, cite bad language!

indicators.note: leaders come at the front, so only the opening letters of the two Houses are taken
something bad is spoilt, so these letters are wrongly ordered

blocks.note: first letter of Commons
first letter of Lords
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A parliamentary row where both Houses' leaders are accused of bad language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad language' suggests swearing in Parliament; the definition is just 'language'. Commons and Lords are the two Houses of the UK Parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: Celtic is the family of languages including Welsh, Irish and Scottish Gaelic, and Breton.

clue.text: A lack of quiet song refrain in rock

indicators.note: 'in' places the refrain inside the stone

blocks.note: sh! is a call for quiet
ore is rock containing metal
a tag is a short repeated closing phrase in a song

explanation.surface: Rock music with no quiet ballads or catchy choruses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock' and 'song' together suggest music, but rock is mineral-bearing stone. A tag is the phrase repeated at a song's close.
explanation.definitionFit: A shortage is a deficiency, a lack of something needed.

clue.text: Ball held by top class residence on the river?

indicators.note: something held by another sits inside its grasp, so one piece goes within

blocks.note: A is the top grade or class
a flat is a home
O is ball-shaped

explanation.surface: A dance held at a smart riverside mansion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ball' looks like a dance, but it is just the round letter O, which goes inside FLAT after A.
explanation.definitionFit: A boat on the river is floating, and the question mark admits the definition is by example.

clue.text: In fact, oil production is legendary

indicators.note: a production makes something new from raw material, so the letters are rebuilt

blocks.note: the letters of these words, taken as written

explanation.surface: A claim that the oil industry's output has become the stuff of legend.
explanation.definitionFit: A legendary figure belongs to stories rather than history, so is invented or made up.

clue.text: Crossing a line in pursuit of farceur

blocks.note: Ben Travers wrote the Aldwych farces
taken as written
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A comic performer being chased across the stage, line in hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In pursuit of' puts A and L after the farceur, who is Ben Travers, the English writer of farces.
explanation.definitionFit: A traversal is the act of going across something, a crossing.

clue.text: Devote time to break useless caddie's resolve finally

indicators.note: breaking into something means getting inside it, so the time goes within
useless suggests a hopeless jumble, so the letters are reordered
finally points to the very last letter of the word

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
T is the abbreviation for time
last letter of resolve

explanation.surface: A golfer urging time be given to shaking an incompetent caddie's resolve.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of caddie's adds nothing; the jumbled CADDIE with E has T inserted before its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To devote time or effort to something is to dedicate it to that purpose.

clue.text: Crusty thing, the poet, Holder

blocks.note: a scab is a crust over a wound
the Bard is Shakespeare, the poet

explanation.surface: A crusty old poet named Holder.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital on Holder disguises it as a surname; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A scabbard is a sheath, a container that holds a sword.

clue.text: Criminal goes to bed unusually on time? It's not worth pursuing

indicators.note: unusually means not in the usual way, so these letters take an odd order

blocks.note: a criminal deed is bad
taken as written, to be rearranged
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A crook unexpectedly turning in early, and a pursuer deciding to give up the chase.
explanation.definitionFit: A bad debt is money owed that cannot be recovered, so chasing it is pointless.

clue.text: Odd, irregular stone's fair feature

indicators.note: irregular means not in regular order, so the letters are reshuffled

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
a gem is a precious stone; the 's adds S

explanation.surface: An oddly shaped stone being the pretty part of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fair' looks like an adjective meaning lovely; it is a funfair.
explanation.definitionFit: Dodgems are bumper cars, a standard ride at a funfair.

clue.text: Turbulent water taking one day to fill pans

indicators.note: filling something means going inside it, so these go within

blocks.note: to pan or rap is to criticise harshly
I is the Roman numeral one
D is the abbreviation for day

explanation.surface: Water churning while a day goes by waiting for pots to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pans' looks like cooking pots, but it is the verb meaning criticises harshly.
explanation.definitionFit: Rapids are stretches of a river where fast water churns over rocks.

clue.text: Meaning to climb up, right and left

indicators.note: climbing goes upward, which in a down clue means the word is read bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written, to be turned round
R is the abbreviation for right
port is the left side of a ship

explanation.surface: Intending to clamber upward, to the right and to the left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Meaning' looks like the verb intending, but the definition is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The purport of a statement is its meaning or general gist.

clue.text: Truss passed water plant

blocks.note: to truss is to tie up, or bind
wee'd, urinated

explanation.surface: A trussed-up person who has wet themselves, or a water plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Water plant' reads as a single aquatic thing; 'water' belongs with 'passed'.
explanation.definitionFit: Bindweed is a climbing plant, convolvulus, that twines round other plants.

clue.text: Villain put away minister

blocks.note: a cur is a scoundrel
to put food away is to eat it

explanation.surface: A crook has jailed a government minister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put away' suggests imprisoned; here it means eaten.
explanation.definitionFit: A curate is an assistant clergyman, a minister of the church.

clue.text: Award I had for Matchmaker role

blocks.note: a cup is a trophy awarded
I'd is short for I had

explanation.surface: An actor collecting a prize for playing a matchmaker.
explanation.definitionFit: Cupid, the Roman god of love, is the archetypal bringer-together of lovers.

clue.text: Effective power of the disheartened and the deranged

indicators.note: losing its heart means the middle goes and only the outside remains
deranged means thrown into disorder, so the letters are mixed up

blocks.note: outer letters of the
the letters of this word, rearranged

explanation.surface: The bite, or real strength, of those who are depressed and those who are mad.
explanation.walkthrough: Both 'the's are wordplay, not articles.
explanation.definitionFit: A law with teeth has real force; teeth idiomatically means power to enforce.

clue.text: If not overcast, going topless

indicators.note: topless means its top is lost, so the first letter is dropped

blocks.note: an overcast day has no sun

explanation.surface: A sunbather saying they will go topless unless it clouds over.
explanation.definitionFit: Unless is a conjunction that means except if, or if not.

clue.text: Crude oil rep, Rex, one gone for a Burton?

indicators.note: crude means rough and unrefined, so the letters come out in a raw new order
'gone' means the one is removed from the letters

blocks.note: the letters of these words, taken as written
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: An oil salesman named Rex who has gone for a Burton, British slang for died.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gone for a Burton' is British slang for killed; here Burton is Sir Richard Burton, the Victorian traveller. 'Crude oil' looks like a pair but only 'Crude' indicates.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Richard Francis Burton was an explorer of Africa and Arabia, so one example of the type.

clue.text: Covering that's unusual for a loft

indicators.note: unusual means not as normal, so the letters are set in a different order

blocks.note: the letters of these words, taken as written

explanation.surface: A surprising sort of top for an attic room.
explanation.definitionFit: A flat roof is the level covering over a building, an unusual shape above a loft.

clue.text: Go on, chuck final!

blocks.note: to last is to go on, continue
to ditch is to throw away

explanation.surface: A fan urging a team on in the final.
explanation.definitionFit: A last-ditch attempt is a final desperate effort, from the last line of defensive trenches.
